issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma in a 34-year-old Navy Officer, 'Known People: Related people' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger without any accompanying memory or appraisal content about bereavement, loss of specific others, or interpersonal aspects of the disaster. The rest of the profile does not explain why related people would be a salient trigger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance shame concerns, but the negative appraisals and memory items do not involve appearance, performance failure, humiliation, or social judgment. This maladaptive strategy appears to address a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

'Avoid Friends' similarly implies socially driven withdrawal, yet the selected appraisals are global despair and alienation rather than fear of specific interpersonal consequences, and the trigger set does not include friendship or social contact themes. It is not impossible, but in combination with 'Avoid Evaluation' it pulls toward a social-evaluative formulation not supported elsewhere.

For a natural-disaster trauma in a Navy officer, 'Similar cars' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the profile. The other triggers are generic situational reminders (crowding, locations), but this item implies a specific vehicle-related cue that is not supported by the trauma type, memory content, or appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are extremely global and severe ('life not worth living', 'belong nowhere') relative to the rest of the selected items, which focus on trauma reminders, fragmented imagery, and avoidance. This creates a coherence problem because the profile lacks corresponding threat content or broader self-concept material to support such pervasive suicidal/existential beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is especially difficult to reconcile with the demographic/contextual profile of a married Navy officer after a natural disaster unless other items indicate moral injury, social alienation, or occupational rupture; none are present in the selected components.

vignette:
Marcus is a 34-year-old Navy officer, married, who presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after surviving a catastrophic hurricane that struck a coastal base where he was stationed. The storm made landfall with little warning during the night, and Marcus spent several hours pinned beneath collapsed structural debris in a flooded utility corridor, surrounded by other personnel, the air thick with the smell of seawater and, later, the sharp chemical bite of alcohol from ruptured medical supply stores nearby. The corridor was dark, the space impossibly cramped, and the press of bodies around him in the chaos was inescapable. He was eventually extracted, physically intact, but the hours he spent in that corridor have not left him.

In the months that followed, Marcus found that the world had become a landscape of landmines. Crowded spaces - the base commissary, the mess hall at peak hours, the narrow passageways aboard ship that are simply part of his working life as a Navy officer - began to carry an unbearable charge. The moment he felt bodies pressing close, or caught the antiseptic edge of alcohol from a colleague cleaning a wound nearby, his memory would detonate: not as a recollection but as a full sensory reinstatement, his body curling slightly, shoulders drawing inward, as though he were still wedged beneath the debris. He reports that the memories arrive mostly as images - vivid, fragmented pictures of the dark corridor, the water rising, the faces around him - and that the experience is so extreme it retains a quality of unreality, as though it happened to someone else, or to a character in a film he cannot stop watching. Yet his body does not agree with that unreality; it responds as though the threat is immediate and present.

These intrusive images, in turn, have begun to shape how Marcus understands himself. When the memories surface, they carry with them a settled conviction that he is no longer who he was - that the person who was easy-going, sociable, and content has been replaced by something diminished and apart. He had come to believe, with quiet certainty, that he no longer belongs anywhere: not fully in his marriage, not among his fellow officers, not in the civilian world his wife inhabits on weekends. This sense of isolation is not merely felt but acted upon. He has progressively withdrawn from friends, declining invitations with vague excuses, and has begun avoiding any circumstance that carries even a faint associative resemblance to the event - he will not enter dark rooms without first flooding them with light, avoids the lower decks of vessels when he can, and routes himself around crowded spaces whenever his duties permit. At work, this has become noticeable; junior officers have remarked on his altered patterns, and his commanding officer has twice asked whether he is managing his duties adequately.

The appraisals themselves have become their own source of triggering. When Marcus registers the feeling of isolation or the conviction that he is permanently changed, his threat sensitivity sharpens, and ordinary environments - a crowded briefing room, a corridor that is slightly too narrow - are perceived through a lens already primed for danger. The negative self-appraisals do not merely follow the memories; they precede and amplify the next encounter with a trigger, so that the loop tightens continuously. Most corrosively, Marcus has come to tell himself that his suffering is deserved - that something in his conduct during those hours, some failure of composure or leadership, means he has no right to feel better. This punishment thinking keeps him from seeking relief and keeps the memories close, as though attending to them is an obligation. The avoidance strategies that were meant to protect him have instead preserved the traumatic material intact, ensuring that nothing is processed and nothing fades.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was his wife's direct statement, delivered quietly one evening, that she felt she had lost him. He arrived at the intake session composed and precise in the way of someone long trained to manage presentation, but described himself as exhausted. What he most fears is that she is right - that the person he used to be is simply gone. What he most hopes, though he expressed it with evident difficulty, is that he might be wrong about that.
